lines: Nib: Ha! Go cry to the guild. They've got a form for that.
Nib: Oi, ferry kid. Nib Wexley. Quay born, quay raised, quay's finest.
Nib: Everyone off that boat thinks they're somebody. Let's see if you are.
Nib: Beginner's luck. The quay always lets tourists win the first one. Then it eats them.
Nib: Guild kid now, are we? Shiny badge. Bet it opens doors and closes mouths.
Nib: Round two. I've been training. Mostly. Bit of napping.
Nib: Fine. FINE. My Riptail had a cramp. It's a known condition.
Nib: Funny running into you out here. Totally by chance. I wasn't following you.
Nib: I was following the reeds. You happen to be standing in them.
Nib: Here's the thing, guild kid. You win too much. People notice. People pay for notes on people like you.
Nib: You still drawing every bend of every road? Neat. Very... useful.
Nib: Don't look at me like that. I'm a businessman now. Small business. Tiny.
Nib: Your notebook is wasted on you. You don't even know what it's worth.
Nib: Took you long enough. The Keeper's down? Good. Saves me the bother.
Nib: Last round, guild kid. Winner takes the hoard. Loser takes the stairs.
Nib: ...Right. Okay. I want you to know this is nothing personal.
Nib: I sold your route notes to the Quay Book three weeks ago. Every bend. Every shortcut.
Nib: Rent's due, kid. Trust no one. Especially the ones who keep showing up.
You hand Nib the notebook you drew for him on purpose. Every road in it ends in a bog.
Nib: The Quay Book bought this. They paid for this. Oh no. Oh, they're going to make me eat it.
Three quay rats step out of the shadows, holding a copy of your own map.
Rat: Nice drawing. Shame about the artist.
The quay rat's notebook
Nib Wexley battled you across Corvane and sold your route notes to the Quay Book.
He called it business. He kept showing up, so you thought he was a friend.
The rats pick your pockets with good manners and better speed. They even leave a receipt.
Mother Gaunt: Gaunt and Daughters. Loans, condolences and gentle reminders.
Mother Gaunt: Four of my clients forgot to pay. Memory is a terrible thing, love. Jog theirs.
Mother Gaunt: Smiler Toft on the quay, Peg Mossop in the fen, Twitchy Ambrose by Stillwater and old Brask up in Greyreach.
Mother Gaunt: All four paid? Look at you. A natural. You've got your mother's... no, I don't know your mother.
Mother Gaunt: Here's your cut. Count it outside. Slowly. Down the dark lane, preferably.
Smiler: Gaunt sent you? I'm smiling, see? This is my paying face. It's also my running face.
Toft: Fine. Fight me for it.
Toft: Take it. Tell Gaunt I said... no. Tell her nothing. She hears everything anyway.
Toft: Paid up. I'm a free man. Poor, but free.
Peg: I borrowed nine coins in spring. Now I owe ninety. Gaunt calls it interest. I call it a crime with paperwork.
Mossop: Fine. Fight me for it.
Mossop: Take it. Tell Gaunt I said... no. Tell her nothing. She hears everything anyway.
Mossop: Paid up. I'm a free man. Poor, but free.
Ambrose: Is she here? Is she behind you? She's always behind someone.
Ambrose: Fine. Fight me for it.
Ambrose: Take it. Tell Gaunt I said... no. Tell her nothing. She hears everything anyway.
Ambrose: Paid up. I'm a free man. Poor, but free.
Brask: Forty years I've owed that woman. It's the longest relationship I've ever had.
Brask: Fine. Fight me for it.
Brask: Take it. Tell Gaunt I said... no. Tell her nothing. She hears everything anyway.
Brask: Paid up. Now listen, because I like your face.
Brask: Gaunt never shares a cut. She sends the Daughters to take it back off whoever collects. Watch the dark lane.
You take the long way round, past the guard house. Two of Gaunt's Daughters wait in the dark lane for nobody.
Mother Gaunt (later): Clever. I hate clever. Keep the cut, love. And never come back for another.
In the dark lane two of Gaunt's Daughters step out, smiling exactly like their mother.
Daughter: Mum says thanks for collecting. Now hand it over.
Gaunt and Daughters
You collected four debts for Mother Gaunt in Madderby.
She paid your cut and sent her daughters to take it back. Brask tried to warn you.
The Daughters count the coins twice and wish you a lovely evening.
Glum: Mortimer Glum, undertaker. Business is dead. Ha. That's my one joke.
Glum: I have a funeral today and no mourners. A funeral with no mourners is just a picnic in black.
Glum: Find me three people who will cry for a fee. Pruett in Madderby, Old Reedy in the fen, and Lettie here on the quay.
Glum: Three mourners! Places, everyone. Lettie, louder. Reedy, less snoring.
Glum: We are gathered here for Bubbles, a Kelpup of great appetite and little sense...
The box wobbles. Bubbles sneezes, climbs out and eats the flowers.
Glum: Well. The service was still performed. That will be the full fee, from you, since you organised it.
Glum: Joking. Mostly. Take this. Funerals are rare. Happy endings are rarer.
Glum: Still short of mourners. The deceased is getting impatient. Metaphorically.
Glum: Bubbles comes by every day now. Eats my flowers. I've started to like him. Don't tell anyone.
Pruett: Cry for a stranger's Kelpup? I've buried three husbands. I can cry on cue.
Pruett: Watch. ...See? Real tears. Tell Glum I charge extra for sobbing.
Pruett: Best funeral I ever went to. Nobody even died.
Pruett: Lovely weather for a funeral. Not that anyone's asked me to one.
Reedy: A funeral? Is there food? There's always food at funerals.
Reedy: Put me down for weeping. Light weeping. My knees can't do the heavy kind.
Reedy: Best funeral I ever went to. Nobody even died.
Reedy: Lovely weather for a funeral. Not that anyone's asked me to one.
Lettie: I cry at everything. Boats. Bread. Nice weather. I'm the best mourner on the quay.
Lettie: Tell Glum I'm coming. I'm already crying a little, see?
Lettie: Best funeral I ever went to. Nobody even died.
Lettie: Lovely weather for a funeral. Not that anyone's asked me to one.
A grey rook feather, stuck in a crack. It looks like it's been waiting for you.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather. Somebody tied a tiny note to it: 'IOU'.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather, tucked behind a crate like contraband.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather on a doorstep. Rooks leave them as rent, they say.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather, floating on a puddle. It's dry when you pick it up.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather in the reeds, pointing the way you came.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather caught on a post. It hums in the wind.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather, bent like a question mark.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather jammed in the rock. A rook watches you take it and says nothing.
You got a grey feather.
A grey rook feather on a gravestone with no name. Cheerful.
You got a grey feather.
Corbin: Corbin. People call me the Featherman. People are not very creative.
Corbin: The rooks of Corvane drop grey feathers all over the river. Bring me twelve and I'll make you something nice.
Corbin: And if you go into the Rook Vault below, mind your guide. Everyone down there works for someone.
Corbin: Twelve! Every one grey as a Monday. Hold still.
Corbin: There. A rook-feather charm. Wear it and the rooks will only steal from other people.
Corbin: Twelve feathers. Grey ones. The black ones are just crows showing off.
Corbin: The rooks have stopped stealing from you, haven't they? Told you.
Corbin: That quay boy, Nib. He sells notebooks to the Quay Book. Other people's notebooks.
Corbin: If he asks to see your map, draw him a bad one. Bog on every corner.
Harbourmaster Quill: Bounties! Four rascals, four posters, four lovely rewards. Minus fees.
Quill: The Wet Rat in the fen, the Dyer's Ghost in Madderby, Knuckles Marrin by Stillwater, Sister Smudge in Greyreach.
Quill: Beat them, I pay you. That's how honest work works. Allegedly.
Quill: All four! The quay sleeps safer. Here's your reward.
Quill: It's half. The other half is the harbour fee, the poster fee, the ink fee and the fee for explaining fees.
Quill: Don't make that face. Everybody on this quay skims. I'm just the only one with a stamp.
Quill: Posters are on the board. Rascals are out there. Fees are in here.
Quill: New poster next week. Same fees. Fees never retire.
Wet Rat: Bounty on me? How much? ...That's insulting. I'm worth twice that.
Wet Rat: Fine. Tell Quill I said his fees are the real crime.
Wet Rat: Go on, collect. I'll be back on a poster by spring.
Ghost: Whooo... okay, I'm not a ghost. I'm a dyer in a sheet. The vats were grey, and the sheet was free.
Dyer's Ghost: Fine. Tell Quill I said his fees are the real crime.
Dyer's Ghost: Go on, collect. I'll be back on a poster by spring.
Knuckles: They call me Knuckles because I crack them. Before battles. It's my warm-up. It's very loud.
Knuckles Marrin: Fine. Tell Quill I said his fees are the real crime.
Knuckles Marrin: Go on, collect. I'll be back on a poster by spring.
Smudge: I forge guild maps. Little smudge here, little smudge there. Tourists walk into lakes. It's art.
Sister Smudge: Fine. Tell Quill I said his fees are the real crime.
Sister Smudge: Go on, collect. I'll be back on a poster by spring.
Fenwick: Lucky Fenwick! Spirling races on the pond! Everybody wins! Mostly me!
Fenwick: Put a stake on your lead Spirling? Fifty coins. Can't lose. Statistically you can, but emotionally you can't.
Fenwick: Fixed? Me? I'm Lucky Fenwick! Luck can't be fixed. It can be arranged, but not fixed.
Fenwick: All right, all right. You want your money back, you take it off my champion.
Fenwick: Lost by a nose! Tragic. The nose was very long. Better luck next time!
Fenwick: New rule: no more races. Now it's 'Spirling Strolling'. Nobody wins. Very fair.
Morag: You bet on Fenwick's race? Oh, love. Oh no.
Morag: I ride for him. He pays me to sneeze at the finish line. Every race. I have the healthiest sneeze in Corvane.
Morag: Go and shake him. Tell him Wee Morag says the sneeze is retiring.
Morag: I'm a jockey. I ride Spirlings in circles and get paid in apologies.
Morag: I'm opening a tea stall. No races. No sneezing. Just tea.
Fenwick: Ow. Fine! Your fifty back, and fifty for your silence. Silence is expensive in Stillwater.
Fenwick: The house always wins! The house is a tent, but still.
Pell: Pockets Pell. I buy, I sell, I forget faces. Professionally.
Pell: Lend me your lead Spirling for one little job on the quay? Clean job. Mostly clean. Back by dusk.
Pell: Pleasure doing business. Or the other thing. I forget which.
Your Spirling comes back by dusk, as promised. Its keepsake does not.
Pell: Fell off. Into my pocket. Gravity, eh?
Pell: Job went smooth. Your Spirling's a natural lookout. Here, a cut. Don't ask what of.
Pell: Back safe, not a scratch. See? Honest crook. Rarest thing on the quay.
Ollie: Ollie Fairweather's Miracle Tonic! Cures colds, grey moods and bad hair!
Ollie: Lend me 250 coins for a new batch and I'll pay you back double. Partners!
Ollie: The secret ingredient is pond water. Don't tell. Nobody believes it anyway.
Ollie's stall is gone. A sign hangs where it stood: 'Closed for personal growth.'
Ollie: The tonic sold out! Turns out people love pond water if it's in a nice bottle. Your share, partner.
Ollie: Sold enough to pay you back. Exactly. Not a coin more. Don't look so surprised.
Miracle Tonic
You lent Ollie Fairweather money for his tonic. He packed up the stall that night.
Quill: You're holding the Quay Book's ledger. In my handwriting. Awkward.
Quill: Fine. I bought the boy's notes. I buy everyone's notes. A harbour runs on knowing who sails where.
Quill: Fees, love. Everything is fees. Even you.
Under a loose plank: a tin box with a stamp on the lid. The Quay Book's drop.
Inside, a note: 'Courier collects at Stillwater, by the north bank. Bring the guild kid's next pages.'

book_drop_idle: A loose plank. Under it, nothing but a very surprised beetle.

lines: Courier: Pages? You're not Nib. Nib is late. Nib is never late, he's greedy.
Courier: Ow. Fine. Take the ledger. I only deliver it. To the stamp. On the quay.
Courier: You know. The stamp. The one who charges for explaining fees.
Courier: The ledger goes to the harbour office. Don't tell him I told you. He'll charge me for it.
Courier: I'm between jobs now. Mostly between hiding places.
Quill: The harbour will need a new harbourmaster. And a new Quay Book. Busy week.
Quill: Take your notes back. Every page. I kept them neat. I'm a professional.
Quill: Thank you for your visit. There is a fee for that too.
The Quay Book
Harbourmaster Quill bought route notes from half of Corvane, Nib's included.
He skimmed your bounties too. Everyone on the quay skims. He just had a stamp.
Vetch: Vetch. Cousin of the dye families. The poor cousin. The clever one.
Vetch: Grey dye is all anyone can get now, so grey dye is gold. Carry a crate to Jory in the Woadfen?
Vetch: Easy coins. No questions. Questions cost extra.
Vetch: Rocks? In my crate? Shocking. Truly. Who would do such a thing?
Vetch: All right. I sold the dye twice and the crate once. That's business, not betrayal. Different word.
Vetch: Grey is the new red. Write that down.
Vetch: I've gone legitimate. I sell maps now. Some of them are even right.
Jory: Vetch's crate? Lovely. Let's see the goods... Rocks. Grey rocks. Painted grey, even.
Jory: He did this to me last month too. I keep hoping. Hope is cheaper than dye.
Jory: Moss-eye Jory. I buy dye, I sell dye, I get rocks. The fen economy.
Vetch: Ow. Fine. Here's your fee, and Jory's money. Tell him the next crate's real. It won't be.
Vetch: See? Questions do cost extra.
Hobb: The Greyreach Ladder. Five tamers up the cliff, each meaner than the last.
Hobb: Beat all five and I'll give you my old belt. It's lucky. I lost it in a bet once, then I won it back.
Hobb: All five rungs! Here. The belt didn't fit, so I sold it. Have this instead.
Hobb: The Ladder doesn't climb itself. Mostly because it's people.
Hobb: Top of the Ladder. Nothing up there but wind and you.
Wren: First rung. The easy one. That's what everyone says about me. They're wrong.
Wren: Go on then. Next rung. Mind the wind.
Wren: Hobb pays me in soup. It's good soup, to be fair.
Tull: Second rung. I'm only here because the first rung owes me money.
Tull: Go on then. Next rung. Mind the wind.
Tull: Hobb pays me in soup. It's good soup, to be fair.
Mabs: Third rung. Halfway up. Halfway down. Depends on your mood.
Mabs: Go on then. Next rung. Mind the wind.
Mabs: Hobb pays me in soup. It's good soup, to be fair.
Orrin: Fourth rung. I've been up here so long the rooks think I'm furniture.
Orrin: Go on then. Next rung. Mind the wind.
Orrin: Hobb pays me in soup. It's good soup, to be fair.
Dorsey: Top rung. Nobody beats me. Mostly because nobody gets this far.
Dorsey: Go on then. Next rung. Mind the wind.
Dorsey: Hobb pays me in soup. It's good soup, to be fair.
Sorrel: Sorrel, naturalist. I'm writing the first honest Spirlog of Corvane. The last one was written by Quill. It had fees.
Sorrel: Bring me Corvane's own kinds in your team: Millwhit, Drizzlet, Reedquill, Puddock, Glimmoth and Silthop.

lines: Sorrel: Show me another. My pencil is getting bored.
Sorrel: Six kinds, all drawn. Next I'll write the rude chapter: Spirlings that bite tourists.
Sorrel: All six! The Spirlog is done. Here's a copy. It's mostly drawings of noses.
Ma Rook: Rook Post. We deliver anything, anywhere, eventually. My rooks are on strike.
Ma Rook: Five letters. Madderby, the fen, Stillwater, Greyreach and one here on the quay. Don't read them. Everybody reads them.
Ma Rook: All five delivered? Even the last one? ...The last one was to my husband. From me. It said 'Come home, the rooks miss you.'
Ma Rook: He's been on the next pier for six years. Pride is a long swim. Here, your wages.
Ma Rook: Letters don't deliver themselves. Neither do rooks, apparently.
Ma Rook: He came home. Brought his own rook. They argue. It's lovely.
Brine: A letter? For me? ...It's from my own tenant. Saying I owe HIM rent. Bold.
Brine: I like him. I'm doubling it.
Brine: Nothing for me today? Good. Letters are just worries with stamps.
Nettle: A love letter! To me? ...No. To Nettle. My sister. Also Nettle. Long story. Parents were tired.
Nettle: Nothing for me today? Good. Letters are just worries with stamps.
Pike: My own letter, sent back. 'Address unknown'. I sent it to myself. Even the post doesn't want me.
Pike: Nothing for me today? Good. Letters are just worries with stamps.
Gale: A letter up here? I moved here so nobody could find me. Who told the rooks?
Gale: It's from my mother. She found me. Of course she found me.
Gale: Nothing for me today? Good. Letters are just worries with stamps.
Haddock: From Ma Rook? Six years and she writes now? ...Fine. Fine! I'll come home. Tell the rook to stop staring.
Haddock: Nothing for me today? Good. Letters are just worries with stamps.
Dimsy: Dimsy Crake, vault guide. I know the Rook Vault like my own pockets. Better. My pockets have holes.
Dimsy: There's a side tunnel to the hoard. Quiet, quick, no rooks. Want me to show you?
Dimsy: The Vault doesn't care who you trust. Neither do I. Have a nice day!
The side tunnel is quiet and quick. At its end two vault robbers are waiting with a lantern and a grin.
Robber: Dimsy sends his love. And his commission.
The side tunnel ends at a dusty crate. Dimsy prises it open and hands you a share. 'Honest guide. Rare breed.'
The side tunnel just leads back to the stairs. Dimsy shrugs. 'Scenic route.'
The robbers take a toll and leave you in the dark, humming.
